sections.h2: What do I need to do to sell a house in Warrington, PA?
sections.html:
In Warrington Township the seller must obtain an Occupancy Certificate before settlement, which means applying at least 30 days ahead, paying $140 per residential unit and passing an inspection. The township puts this duty on the seller or landlord, and a real estate agent or other representative may file on the seller's behalf. After that, the sale follows the usual Pennsylvania disclosure, tax and deed-recording sequence.

Warrington is a Bucks County township of 13.7 square miles with an estimated 26,261 residents. Its motto calls it the Gateway to Historic Bucks County, and the township was founded in October 1734 and named for Warrington, England. Its population grew from 2,336 in 1950 to 25,639 in 2020, so a large share of its houses date from the 1980s through the 2000s, the years when the count rose from 10,704 to 23,418.

sections.h2: How does the Warrington occupancy certificate work?
sections.html:
The certificate is a township inspection that confirms a home meets safety and property maintenance requirements before it changes hands. The Permits Office takes applications online or by mail or drop-off at the township building, and the applicant is responsible for making sure the fee is paid and the inspection is scheduled.

The township's program page sets out these terms:

  • Apply at least 30 days before settlement so there is time to fix problems the inspection finds.
  • The residential fee is $140 per unit. Confirm commercial fees before you submit.
  • A certificate is valid for 60 days from the date it is issued, so do not schedule the inspection months before closing.
  • Homes with fire sprinkler systems need a separate inspection and certification by a registered third-party agency, and that sprinkler certification is valid for six months.
  • The township publishes a residential inspection checklist, so you can walk the house before the inspector does.

If a sale falls through and the certificate expires, you would have to apply again for the next buyer. Build that risk into your timeline if your buyer needs financing.

sections.h2: What do Census figures show for Warrington housing?
sections.html:
Warrington has the most expensive owner-occupied housing of the four townships in this Census comparison, and the highest owner rate. The Census Bureau's QuickFacts give these figures.

With 92.5 percent of residents in the same house a year earlier, turnover is the lowest of the group. A buyer here is often a family relocating for the school district, so a clean inspection result and a clear certificate carry weight.

sections.h2: What is the Warrington area like for buyers?
sections.html:
Warrington is a suburb of winding creeks and commuter roads, and buyers compare it on schools, drive time and storm drainage. Natural features include the Little Neshaminy Creek, Mill Creek, Park Creek, Fretz Valley, Griers Hill and Prospect Hill. Villages within the township are Warrington, Neshaminy, Tradesville, Eureka, Frog Hollow and Palomino Farms.

Public schools are part of the Central Bucks School District: Barclay, Mill Creek and Titus elementary schools, Tamanend Middle School and Central Bucks High School South. Neighbors include New Britain, Doylestown, Warwick, Warminster, Horsham and Montgomery townships.

  • US 202 runs through the western part of the township as a parkway, and PA 611 (Easton Road) crosses the eastern side.
  • PA 152 (Limekiln Pike), PA 132 (Street Road), Lower State Road and County Line Road connect the neighborhoods.
  • The township maintains 83.51 of its 102.37 miles of public roads.
  • SEPTA City Bus Route 55 follows PA 611, and the DART South bus runs weekdays along the same corridor to Doylestown.

Warrington has also had a local fight over land use. In 2010 a pharmaceutical company proposed the largest warehouse facility in Pennsylvania near residential neighborhoods in the township, residents objected loudly, and the company chose a site in Northeast Philadelphia instead. Buyers who care about open land and traffic remember that history, and the township's zoning rules decide what can be built near your street. If a buyer asks about nearby development, point them to the township's Planning and Zoning staff, who work with the Bucks County Planning Commission on zoning updates, and keep a copy of your own survey and any permit records for the closing file.

The humid continental climate brings about 47 inches of precipitation a year, with July the wettest month and seasonal snowfall of 30 to 36 inches. Wet basements and roof wear are therefore the questions inspectors ask most.

sections.h2: What taxes and disclosures apply when I sell in Warrington?
sections.html:
Bucks County's recorder says the transfer tax on a Pennsylvania sale is 2 percent, 1 percent to the state and 1 percent to the municipality and school district, paid when the deed is recorded. The recorder no longer accepts personal checks for it; cash in the office, a cashier's check, a money order or a credit card will do. Sellers and buyers usually divide the tax by agreement, and a family transfer may be exempt with a Statement of Value form where the deed does not state the exemption.

The disclosure rule is in 68 Pa.C.S. Section 7303. Before the agreement of sale is signed, you deliver a signed property disclosure statement covering the roof, basement, drainage, plumbing, wiring and similar items. Act 74 of 2026 adds a flood-insurance notice that sellers provide once the Insurance Department posts its flood information, which matters in a township with several creeks.

For assessment, the Bucks Board of Assessment Appeals set August 3, 2026 as the 2026 annual appeal deadline, and that date has passed. Annual appeal changes apply to the following tax year. The homestead and farmstead exclusion filing deadline is March 1 for the tax year that starts July 1. A new owner must send contact information to the Board within 30 days of buying, so remind your buyer.

sections.h2: Should I fix the house, list it or sell as-is in Warrington?
sections.html:
Warrington's high median values reward a well-presented house, but the 30-day occupancy lead time and a sprinkler certification, if you have one, can slow a quick listing. A cash buyer who accepts the house as-is still has to see the township certificate handled before settlement, so ask how that works before you agree to a date.

  • Apply for the occupancy certificate as soon as you have a contract, not at the closing table.
  • Walk the township checklist yourself and fix cheap items first.
  • Compare a listing net sheet with a cash offer that states who pays for repairs the inspector requires.

faqs.q: How much is the occupancy certificate in Warrington?
faqs.a: The township charges $140 per unit for residential properties. Commercial fees differ, and the township asks you to confirm the amount before submitting.

faqs.q: How long does a Warrington occupancy certificate last?
faqs.a: It is valid for 60 days from the date it is issued. If settlement slips past that window, you will need a new certificate.

faqs.q: Who applies for the certificate when a house is sold?
faqs.a: The seller or landlord is responsible, and an agent or authorized representative can file for the seller. The certificate has to be in hand before settlement.

faqs.q: What is the median home value in Warrington?
faqs.a: Owners in Warrington report a midpoint value of $553,100 for 2020 to 2024, the highest of the four townships in the same QuickFacts table.

faqs.q: Does my sprinkler system change anything?
faqs.a: Yes. Houses with fire sprinklers need a separate inspection and certification by a registered third-party agency before the occupancy certificate can be issued, and the sprinkler certification lasts six months. The township posts a list of registered agencies.
